arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Fletcher argued the government may not use coercive threats. He emphasized the distinction between persuasion and coercion.
Aguiñaga argued government censorship has no place in democracy. He cited a large record showing unrelenting pressure on platforms.
Fletcher addressed standing and the merits of the case. He clarified specific emails in the joint appendix.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the limits of government power over private speech. Missouri seeks to stop federal pressure on platforms. The government defends its right to speak freely.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: Missouri wants the Court to strike down the lower court ruling. It seeks to stop federal officials from coercing platforms.
The government wants the Court to uphold its actions. It seeks to confirm its right to persuade private speakers.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: Missouri argues federal officials used coercive threats. It claims this suppressed protected speech on private platforms.
The government argues it only informed and persuaded. It claims this distinction protects its First Amendment rights.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Thomas asked about the constitutional basis for government speech. He questioned the application of state action doctrine.
Justice Sotomayor asked how the injunction harms the government. She sought specifics on the meaning of significant encouragement.
